content: The efficacy of Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) preparations is determined by the larval count 24 hours after the test begins, while the toxicity of Bacillus sphaericus (Bsph) is assessed based on the larval count after 48 hours of exposure. To ensure accuracy, bioassays should be conducted on at least three separate days, alongside a reference standard assay, and the standard deviation of the means should be calculated. A test series is considered valid if the relative standard deviation (RSD) or coefficient of variation (CV) is less than 25%. For the production of test larvae, early fourth-instar larvae are ideal as they represent the overall sensitivity of the target population and are easy to handle. It is crucial to use a homogeneous population of early fourth-instar larvae, which can be obtained within five days of hatching using standardized rearing methods. For Aedes aegypti, eggs are laid in a cup lined with filter paper and filled one-third with deionized water. The paper is dried at room temperature and stored in a sealed plastic bag for several months. When larvae are needed, the paper is immersed in dechlorinated water. To synchronize hatching, larval feed is added to the water 24 hours before adding the eggs. Bacterial growth deoxygenates the water, triggering egg hatching, which typically occurs within 12 hours. The larvae are then transferred to a container with 2 liters of dechlorinated water to achieve a population of 500 to 700 larvae per container. Larval feed, such as protein flakes for aquarium fish or powdered cat biscuits, is provided, and the containers are maintained at 25 ± 2°C. The amount of food must be kept low to prevent excessive bacterial growth, which can kill the larvae. Feeding at intervals of one or two days and daily observation of the larvae is optimal. If the water becomes turbid, it should be replaced by filtering out the larvae and transferring them to a clean container with fresh water and feed. After five to seven days, a homogeneous population of early fourth-instar larvae (5 days old and 4 to 5 mm in length) should be obtained. For Culex pipiens pipiens larvae, obtaining a homogeneous population of fourth instars is more challenging. A large number of egg rafts must be laid and collected on the same day. These can be stored at 15–18°C to accumulate more eggs for hatching. First instars are fragile and should not be handled. Development to the second instar usually takes 3–4 days at 25 ± 2°C after the eggs are laid. When ready, second instars are grouped in a tray with 3 liters of dechlorinated water at a depth of 4–6 cm, with 800–1000 larvae per tray. Food (yeast extract and dog or cat biscuits) is provided as needed. Early fourth instars suitable for testing are usually obtained within 7 days, though sometimes 8 or 9 days are required. The maximum acceptable levels of microbial contaminants have not yet been determined. Fly larvae toxicity tests, such as those described by Bond R.P. et al. in The Thermostable Exotoxin of Bacillus thuringiensis (1971), are not required if the manufacturer has demonstrated that the Bacillus thuringiensis strain does not produce beta-exotoxin. Similarly, no test is required for Bacillus sphaericus, as this species is not known to produce exotoxins. The water content of microbial larvicides should not exceed 5% to prevent premature degradation of the product. The mass of the sample used in the test should be at the highest rate of use recommended by the supplier. Bioassay is the only fully reliable method to measure the mass of active ingredient in suspension. However, simpler methods, such as gravimetric determination, may be used routinely if they have been shown to yield results equivalent to those of the bioassay method. In case of dispute, the bioassay method shall serve as the referee method. Microbial larvicides should be stored at cool temperatures, but accelerated storage stability tests are recommended for rapid checks on product stability. Currently, no standardized method exists for such tests. In the absence of an accelerated storage stability test, the following minimum standards are recommended: a) no more than 10% loss in biopotency below the labeled potency value when stored at 5°C for 2 years; and b) no more than 10% loss in biopotency below the labeled potency value when stored at 20–25°C for 1 year. These tests should be performed using representative product samples, and biopotency should be assessed using the test method described in Note 4. Results from the biopotency test may vary by up to ±25% from the average, and this must be considered when determining potency loss. If oneand two-year test data are not available at the time of drafting a specification, an estimate of storage stability may be acceptable, pending completion of the tests. The bioassay method measures biopotency by comparing mosquito larval mortality caused by the test product with that caused by a reference standard. Biopotency is expressed in International Toxic Units (ITU) per mg of product. Two internationally recognized reference powders are available for determining biopotency using bioassays of bacterial preparations on mosquito larvae. The biopotency of Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti)-based products is compared against a lyophilized reference powder (IPS 82, strain 1884) using early fourth-instar larvae of Aedes aegypti (strain Bora Bora). The toxicity of IPS 82 has an arbitrarily assigned value of 15,000 ITU/mg powder against this insect strain. The biopotency of Bacillus sphaericus (Bsph)-based products is determined against a lyophilized reference powder (SPH 88, strain 2362) using early fourth-instar larvae of Culex pipiens pipiens (strain Montpellier). The toxicity of SPH 88 has an arbitrarily assigned value of 1,700 ITU/mg powder against this insect strain. The toxicity of all bacterial preparations based on Bti or Bsph can be determined against these standard powders. The toxicity (ITU/mg) of tested products is calculated using the formula: Titer (ITU/mg) of tested product = Titer standard (ITU/mg) × LC50 (mg/L) standard ÷ LC50 (mg/L) unknown. The use of alternative bacterial larvicide reference powders or mosquito strains in this test must be approached cautiously, as different results are inevitable. Such alternatives must undergo careful cross-calibration against the reference powders and strains identified above. Ideally, cross-calibration should be conducted by a group of independent expert laboratories. The alternative powders/strains and supporting cross-calibration data should be made available to anyone wishing to use or verify the test with the alternative powders/strains.
